content.intro: Learn string aggregation and summary text through a short explanation, a concept diagram, and a PostgreSQL-oriented example. Focus on the reason for the query or design decision before memorizing syntax.
content.why_it_matters: String Aggregation and Summary Text matters because database behavior becomes more reliable when the intended row meaning, data shape, and edge cases are explicit. This lesson follows the SQL curriculum's listed subtopics and calls out PostgreSQL-specific behavior when it matters.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: In string aggregation and summary text, define the unit of analysis before writing the query: one row per customer, order, day, or other grain. Make filters, NULL handling, time boundaries, and tie-breaking rules visible in the SQL.

content_blocks.title: Apply the idea
content_blocks.text: Start with the subtopics: Combining values across rows, Ordering aggregated strings, Distinct string aggregation where supported, Handling NULL values. Define the result you expect, run or inspect the small example in your own disposable PostgreSQL lab, and change one assumption at a time. The embedded lesson editor is a demonstration shell: the current project shows the sample expected output and does not execute arbitrary SQL on the server.

items.title: Combining values across rows
items.text: Combining values across rows helps you use SQL for reporting and analysis with the right grain, time buckets, windows, distribution statistics, and business metric definitions. Start with a concrete example, state the expected result, and verify the behavior before extending the query or design.

items.title: Ordering aggregated strings
items.text: Ordering aggregated strings summarizes rows. Decide the grain of the result first, group only by the dimensions that define one output row, and verify NULL and duplicate behavior in each metric.

items.title: Distinct string aggregation where supported
items.text: Distinct string aggregation where supported depends on text representation, collation, wildcard semantics, and sometimes locale. Test spaces, case, accents, Unicode, and special characters rather than assuming every database compares strings identically.

items.title: Handling NULL values
items.text: Handling NULL values requires deliberate handling of absent or unknown values. In SQL, NULL is not the same as zero or an empty string; use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL for direct tests and check how expressions and aggregates propagate unknowns.

items.title: Dialect-specific aggregate functions
items.text: Dialect-specific aggregate functions summarizes rows. Decide the grain of the result first, group only by the dimensions that define one output row, and verify NULL and duplicate behavior in each metric.

content_blocks.code:
SELECT customer_id,
       TRIM(full_name) AS clean_name,
       LOWER(email) AS normalized_email,
       LENGTH(full_name) AS name_length
FROM customers
ORDER BY customer_id;
content_blocks.expected_output: The query trims display whitespace and calculates lowercase email and string length without changing stored values.

content_blocks.reset_steps: For queries, restore the original text and compare results. For statements that change data, use the transaction and rollback shown in the example, or recreate the disposable lab from the included setup instructions. Do not reset production data.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.
